title: Predictive locality failover controller with capacity-driven soft-throttles
creator: Maya Thompson
description:
Goal: implement a controller that proactively routes and gracefully fails over multi-region requests using short-horizon capacity forecasts, latency SLO weighting, and soft throttles (token shedding) to avoid abrupt circuit-breaker trips.

Background: current region steering reacts to instantaneous capacity and latency signals which often causes noisy failovers and long tail latency spikes when scheduled maintenance or sudden VM preemptions occur. We want a middle ground: predictive soft-fallbacks that (1) prefer home-region affinity to preserve locality, (2) apply small, evidence-driven reroutes to nearby regions before hard shedding, and (3) only open circuit-breakers when predictive signals indicate sustained degradation.

Key components:
- Short-horizon capacity predictor: lightweight exponential smoothing over per-region free-GPU token buckets + autoscaler queue depth signals.
- SLO-weighted score: combine predicted p95 latency delta, remaining capacity margin, and customer SLO weight to produce region preference scores.
- Soft-throttle layer: per-customer soft token shedding with gradual windowed increase; exposes a probabilistic reroute fraction instead of immediate rejection.
- Graceful circuit-breaker policy: multi-step state machine (Healthy -> Degraded -> Soft-Shed -> Hard-Shed) with separate timers and hysteresis to avoid flip-flopping.
- Telemetry and guardrails: traceable decision reasons attached to routing headers, per-route SLO impact estimator, and an emergency manual override in Console.

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end routing decision executes within 2ms median on the request path (excluding network RTT).
- In fault-injection tests (region capacity drop to 15%), client-side p95 increase limited to <25% compared to baseline; overall successful reroute rate > 95% with soft-throttle engaged.
- No customer experiences hard-shed (HTTP 503) for more than 60s during simulated maintenance if a compatible model variant exists in another region.
- Observability: Console shows per-region predicted capacity, routing fractions, and a decision reason string for >=99% of routed requests.

Design trade-offs and notes:
- We prioritize low-latency decision execution: the predictor uses O(1) updates and bounded history (max 1 minute) to avoid CPU pressure in the dispatcher.
- We prefer probabilistic soft-sharding over deterministic evictions to reduce correlated failures across tenants. This increases variance but reduces tail risk.
- Plan to use existing KV cache compatibility mapping to ensure reroutes only happen to compatible model variants; otherwise the system should fall back to soft-shed rather than cross-model reroute.
